summary: Describes stateful NAT64, which lets IPv6-only clients reach IPv4 servers using unicast UDP, TCP or ICMP by sharing public IPv4 addresses. With DNS64, usually no changes are needed on the client or server. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Stateful NAT64 translates traffic between IPv6 clients and IPv4 servers and remembers mappings so replies return to the right client. DNS64 can provide the IPv6-form address that directs a client to the translator.

questions: how can ipv6 only clients reach ipv4 servers

how can ipv6 clients reach ipv4 servers
subtitle: How an IPv6-only client can start connections to IPv4 servers through a translator.

tldr.problem: An IPv6-only client may need to communicate with an IPv4-only server, while IPv4 addresses are shared among multiple clients.
tldr.mechanism: A stateful NAT64 translates packet headers and records mappings between IPv6 transport addresses and addresses and ports from its IPv4 pool.
tldr.outcome: Together with DNS64, this can let IPv6-only clients reach IPv4-only servers without changes to either endpoint. The RFC specifies unicast TCP, UDP and ICMP query translation.

today: RFC 6146 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is designed to work with RFC 6147 and RFC 6145.

sections.title: What Stateful NAT64 Does
sections.content:
Stateful NAT64 supports communication from IPv6-only clients to IPv4-only servers. With DNS64, a DNS server can synthesize an IPv6 address from the IPv4 address of a server. The NAT64 translates packet headers using the IP/ICMP translation algorithm in RFC 6145.

The specification covers unicast TCP, UDP and ICMP. It does not cover multicast, SCTP, DCCP or IPsec. Without existing state or a configured binding, only an IPv6 node can initiate a session toward an IPv4 node.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT64 translates packets so IPv6-only clients can reach IPv4 servers. In the usual case, the client starts the connection and the translator remembers how to return replies.

sections.title: An IPv6 Client Opens an IPv4 Connection
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, H1 at 2001:db8::1 looks up H2 at IPv4 address 192.0.2.1. DNS64 returns the synthetic address 64:ff9b::192.0.2.1, using the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96.

H1 sends a TCP SYN from port 1500. The NAT64 selects port 2000 on its IPv4 address 203.0.113.1, records the mapping from (2001:db8::1,1500) to (203.0.113.1,2000), translates the packet and forwards it. The reply matches this mapping and is translated back to H1.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator assigns the client's connection an address and port from its IPv4 pool. It uses the saved mapping to send the server's reply back to the correct IPv6 client.

sections.title: Binding and Session Tables
sections.content:
The RFC describes six conceptual tables: a Binding Information Base (BIB) and a session table for each of TCP, UDP and ICMP queries. A TCP or UDP BIB entry maps one IPv6 transport address to one IPv4 transport address. One BIB entry can support multiple sessions.

A session entry also records the remote endpoint and a lifetime. It lets the NAT64 track when a conversation ends and apply address-dependent filtering. Dynamically created BIB entries are removed when their last session ends; manually configured entries remain until an administrator removes them.
sections.plainLanguage: The BIB records which IPv4 address and port stand for a client. A separate session record tracks each conversation and how long its mapping should remain available.

sections.title: Packet Processing and TCP State
sections.content:
The NAT64 identifies an incoming tuple, checks filtering rules and updates its tables, computes an outgoing tuple, translates the packet and handles hairpinning. For TCP, UDP and ICMP errors, a tuple uses source and destination addresses, ports and protocol. For an ICMP query, it uses source, destination and ICMP identifier.

The TCP state machine tracks setup, established traffic, FINs from either side, resets and timeouts. A TCP SYN from the IPv6 side creates state and enters V6 INIT; a matching SYN from IPv4 moves it to ESTABLISHED. A reset enters TRANS for a short period before the state closes or returns to ESTABLISHED.
sections.plainLanguage: For each packet, the translator checks its saved records, applies filtering and rewrites the addresses and ports. It tracks TCP setup and shutdown so it knows when a mapping can be removed.

sections.title: IPv4 Address Representation and Timers
sections.content:
The algorithm that places an IPv4 address in an IPv6 address must be reversible. The prefix length must be at most 96 bits. A NAT64 must support the address construction algorithm in RFC 6052; if no prefix is configured, it should use 64:ff9b::/96.

The RFC sets UDP session lifetimes of at least 2 minutes, with a default of 5 minutes. Established TCP state uses the 2-hour TCP_EST timer plus a 4-minute transition timer. ICMP query state has a 60-second default, and fragment storage must allow fragments to arrive over at least 2 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: A fixed, reversible rule lets the translator recover an IPv4 address from its IPv6 form. Timers limit how long the translator keeps records for UDP, TCP, ICMP and fragments.

sections.title: Security and Resource Limits
sections.content:
Some IPsec protections are incompatible with address translation because they protect header information that NAT64 changes. The RFC says the translation device must protect its limited IPv4 addresses, memory and processing resources from exhaustion attacks. For example, an attacker could send many fragments or SYN packets to consume state.

Filtering determines which incoming IPv4 packets can reach an IPv6 client; address mapping alone does not provide that protection. The NAT64 MUST discard IPv6 packets whose source address falls within its translation prefix, which prevents a hairpinning loop.
sections.plainLanguage: NAT64 changes packet headers, so some end-to-end IPsec checks fail. The translator also needs limits and filtering to stop attackers from exhausting its address pool or state.
